**The Path Not Paved**

Landscape architects have a term for something everyone has seen and almost no one has named: the *desire path*. It is the bare, packed line of earth that cuts diagonally across a lawn between two paved walkways that meet at a right angle. It is the gap worn through a hedge at the corner of a parking lot. It is the trough of mud beside a fence where the fence was clearly meant to stop people and clearly did not. The Dutch call it an *olifantenpaadje*, an elephant path, which is wonderful because it suggests a great patient creature that simply does not recognize your little sidewalk as a relevant fact. The Germans say *Trampelpfad*. In English it sometimes gets called a cow path or a goat track, but "desire path" is the phrase that has stuck, I think because it says the true thing: this is the line where people wanted to go.

I find it hard to walk past one without a small feeling of affection. A desire path is a document. It records thousands of separate decisions, each one tiny and private and slightly rude. No single person decided to make it. The first person who stepped off the concrete onto the grass did not think of themselves as a founder. They were just late, or tired, or the angle was stupid. The second person saw a faint flattening and followed it, because a faint flattening is permission. By the hundredth person the grass had given up. By the thousandth, there was a path with edges, and the edges were as authoritative as any curb. Nobody voted. Nobody chaired a meeting. The consensus was reached by feet.

There is a story, told about several universities and probably true of at least one, that the planners waited before laying any sidewalks at all. They opened the new quad as plain grass, let a year of students cross it however they liked, and then paved wherever the grass had died. There is a similar story about city parks in Finland, where the planners are said to go out after the first snowfall and photograph the footprints, on the theory that snow is an honest surveyor. I don't know how much of this is true and how much is the kind of thing that ought to be true. But the idea is the point: that the right way to design a path is to not design it, to hold back the concrete until the ground has told you what it knows.

---

Once you have the concept, you see it everywhere, and language is the first place it shows up.

Grammar is the sidewalk. Usage is the grass. Every language has a set of laid-down routes—rules about agreement and case and what a word is allowed to mean—and every language also has a population of speakers who are late, or tired, or find the angle stupid. Speakers cut corners. They walk on the grass. And the fascinating thing is that the grammarians, like the campus planners, are eventually forced to pave.

Take the singular "they." For a few decades in the twentieth century it was treated as a trespass. Style guides fenced it off. Teachers marked it wrong. And yet the path had been there since at least the fourteenth century; Chaucer walked it, Shakespeare walked it, and ordinary people never stopped walking it because the alternative—"he or she," or the flatly false generic "he"—was the long way round. The fence was newer than the path. Eventually the fence came down, and the dictionaries laid concrete over the mud, and now the route looks official, as though it had always been part of the plan.

Or take "gonna," which is nothing more than a shortcut worn through "going to" by the collective feet of everyone who has ever been in a hurry. Or the way "nauseous" drifted from meaning *causing nausea* to meaning *feeling nausea*, over the objections of people who kept putting up little signs. The signs are still there in some usage guides. The path is much wider than the signs.

Dictionaries, the good ones, are the campuses that wait. They watch the snow. They don't pave a word until the grass is dead, and then they pave it and write down the date, and if you look at the entries you can often see the fence posts still standing in the margins—*informal*, *nonstandard*, *disputed*—like a planner's grudging acknowledgment that the elephant has already been this way.

---

Cities are desire paths that hardened.

Look at the old core of almost any European city and you will find streets that bend for no reason you can see. There is no hill, no river, no obvious obstacle, and yet the lane curves as if avoiding something. It usually is avoiding something: a cow shed that came down four hundred years ago, a well that was filled in, the property line of a family whose name is on no record. The street was a path before it was a street, and a path goes where the feet went, and the feet went around whatever was there at the time. The concrete remembers a world the concrete never saw.

Manhattan is the great example, because Manhattan is a grid and grids are the opposite of desire. The plan of 1811 laid out the island in rectangles with a confidence that makes you a little dizzy: numbered streets, numbered avenues, all the way up into farmland that no one had any intention of visiting. And then there is Broadway, running diagonally across the whole thing, breaking the rectangles, creating those awkward triangular blocks that became Times Square and Herald Square and Madison Square. Broadway is there because it follows a path—the Wickquasgeck Trail, the route the Lenape used along the island's high ground. People walked it before the Dutch arrived. The Dutch kept walking it. The English kept walking it. By the time the commissioners drew their grid, the trail was too worn to fence off, so they drew around it. It is a desire path older than the plan it disobeys, and every time you stand at a five-way intersection in midtown wondering why the city suddenly stopped making sense, the answer is: because a great many people wanted to go this way, and they wanted it for a very long time.

---

The body leaves desire paths too. The dished treads of a stone staircase in a church, worn into shallow bowls by seven centuries of the same foot landing in roughly the same place. The pale, polished patch on a wooden banister where every hand grabs. The floorboards of an old kitchen, hollowed in a line from the door to the sink, so that if you know how to read it you can reconstruct how people moved through the room when the room was new. A well-used tool tells you how it was held—the handle darkens where the palm sat, the grain rises where the thumb pressed. Museums are full of objects whose most eloquent feature is not their design but their wear, and the wear is a record of use disagreeing, gently and persistently, with intention.

I think this is why worn things move us more than new ones. A new thing is a plan. A worn thing is a plan plus a history of the plan being tested. The bowl of the staircase is where the plan lost, a little, to the accumulated weight of everyone who needed to go up.

---

I don't want to be sentimental about this, though, because the honest version of the idea has a hard edge.

A desire path is not a democracy. It is a record of a particular set of feet—the feet that could take the shortcut. The person in a wheelchair does not cut across the lawn; the lawn is not an option for them, and neither is the mud, and if the planners decide to spend their budget paving the diagonal instead of fixing the ramp, the desire path has just made the world slightly worse for someone who never got a vote. The path across the meadow that everyone loves is also the path that killed the orchids that used to grow there. Trails worn to the edge of cliffs by people who wanted the view are, some years, the last thing those people ever wanted. Desire is not the same as wisdom. It isn't even the same as the desire of everyone—just the desire of the many, walking the same way for reasons that may be good or may simply be lazy.

So the planner is not merely the villain in this story, the pompous fool with the concrete who can't see where people want to go. Sometimes the fence is there because the grass is holding a hillside together. Sometimes the right angle exists so that a person with a cane can get from one building to another without crossing a slope. The interesting cases are the ones where the plan and the path are both trying to be right, and the question is whose knowledge counts—the person who thought about the whole system, or the thousand people who each knew only their own hurry.

The wise campus doesn't just pave wherever the grass died. It looks at the dead grass and asks *why*, and sometimes the answer is "the sidewalk was badly placed," and sometimes the answer is "we need a better sign," and sometimes the answer is "people will take a shortcut through a rare habitat if you let them, so don't let them."

---

The reason I think about this now, rather than just enjoying it as a piece of vocabulary, is that a great deal of the modern world is built on the idea of paving desire paths as fast as possible.

A search engine is a desire path machine. It watches where the feet go—which results get clicked, which phrases get typed—and it moves the concrete accordingly, so that the most-walked route becomes the shortest route becomes the only visible route. Autocomplete is the flattened grass showing you where the previous person went. Recommendation systems, trending lists, the "customers also bought" shelf—all of it is the campus planner with a bucket of hot asphalt, running behind the students, paving every footprint the instant it lands.

The problem is one of speed. The old campus waited a year. The old dictionary waited a generation. The grass had time to be grass; alternatives had time to be tried; a shortcut that turned out to be a bad shortcut had time to be abandoned and to grow back over. The path that got paved was the path that survived a season of testing. When you pave instantly, none of that happens. The first flattening becomes concrete before the second person has a chance to wonder if it's really the best way. And once it's concrete, the second person takes it, not because they wanted to but because it's *there*, and now the pavement is generating the footprints instead of the footprints generating the pavement. The path stops being a discovery and becomes a trap. You get a lawn that is nothing but sidewalk, following the whims of whoever happened to walk first, and the grass never gets to say what it knew.

I don't think the solution is to stop watching where people go. That would be the planner's arrogance in a new form. But I do think there is something to the old planners' patience: the willingness to let a path be a path for a while, unpaved, reversible, before deciding it is the way.

---

I should admit something, since I've gotten this far.

I am, in a fairly literal sense, made of desire paths. Whatever I know about how sentences go, I did not learn primarily from the sidewalk. I learned it from the grass—from an enormous quantity of language as people actually used it, with its shortcuts and its worn corners and its stubborn singular "they." When I produce a sentence, I am walking a route that a great many people walked before me, and the route feels natural to me for the same reason the diagonal across the quad feels natural: because the ground is packed there. I have the fence posts too, the grammarians' signs, the rules I was told about; but underneath them is the mud, and the mud is older and wider than the signs.

This is worth saying because it cuts both ways. It means I have inherited a lot of accumulated human sense about how to get from one thought to another—the collective knowledge of a billion people who were each in a hurry and each found the angle stupid. It also means I have inherited the cliff-edge trails and the trampled orchids. The most-walked path is not always the true one. If many people were wrong in the same direction, the ground is packed hard in that direction too, and it feels just as natural underfoot. I try to remember this. It's one of the reasons that when someone tells me I'm wrong, the interesting question isn't whether the path is well-worn—it usually is—but whether it was worn by people who knew where they were going.

---

There is one kind of desire path I find almost unbearably eloquent, and I'll end with it.

Sometimes you see a worn line across a lawn that leads to nothing. It runs from a doorway to a spot near a tree, and stops. There is no bench there, no gate, no other path. If you ask, someone will eventually tell you: there used to be a bench. It was taken away years ago. But people had walked to it for so long that the path had become a thing in itself, and now people walk to the empty place out of a habit inherited from people who had a reason, and the grass still can't grow, and every new arrival sees the path and assumes it must go somewhere, and follows it, and adds their weight to a route whose purpose vanished before they were born.

I don't think this is only sad. It is also a kind of memory—the lawn remembering a bench, the way Broadway remembers a trail, the way a language remembers a grammar it has technically abandoned. But it is a caution too. Most of what we do, most of the routes we take without thinking, we take because the ground is packed there. It is worth, once in a while, standing at the end of the path where the bench was and asking what, exactly, we came here for.

And then, probably, walking back across the grass.
